nameStory: The 'perennial cornflower' gets its name from its resemblance to the classic cornflower that grows in grain fields, but unlike its annual cousin, this mountain native comes back year after year. 'Cornflower' originally referred to flowers that grew among corn (grain) crops in Europe, though this perennial species prefers mountain meadows to farm fields.
description: Perennial cornflower is a sturdy wildflower that escaped from gardens to naturalize across New England. It produces distinctive bright blue-purple flowers with spiky, fringed petals that look almost like tiny fireworks. Growing 1-2 feet tall, this European mountain native forms spreading clumps and blooms from late spring through summer.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright blue-purple flowers with deeply fringed, spiky outer petals surrounding a darker center, typically one large flower head per stem (occasionally 2-3). The petals feel papery and have an almost feathery texture.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Gray-green leaves are usually entire (not toothed or lobed) and feel slightly fuzzy or woolly to the touch. Lower leaves are lance-shaped while upper leaves are narrower.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms spreading clumps 12-28 inches tall with sturdy, upright stems. Plants spread by underground runners, creating colonies over time.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Stems are ridged with narrow, leaf-like wings running down from where leaves attach. The stems feel firm and slightly angular rather than perfectly round.

habitat: Look for perennial cornflower in disturbed areas, roadsides, field edges, and abandoned gardens where it has escaped cultivation. It prefers well-drained soils and full to partial sun, often appearing in meadows and open areas. This European native adapts well to various soil types but seems to favor slightly alkaline conditions.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges in early spring with gray-green fuzzy leaves forming low rosettes. Flower buds begin developing on stems by late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from May through August with brilliant blue-purple flowers most abundant in early summer. Spent flowers produce small, bristly seeds.
seasonality.fall: Plants may continue blooming sporadically into early fall. Leaves begin to yellow and seeds disperse, often carried by wind.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back, but roots and spreading underground runners remain alive, ready to produce new growth in spring.

funFact: This mountain wildflower is such an enthusiastic escape artist that it's considered invasive in British Columbia, spreading so successfully from gardens that it now threatens native plant communities across entire valleys.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with annual cornflower (bachelor's button), but perennial cornflower typically has just one large flower per stem while annual cornflower has many smaller flowers. Remember: 'One and done' for perennial (one big flower), 'many and annual' for the annual type.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'cornflower,' this plant has nothing to do with corn (maize). The name comes from the European use of 'corn' to mean any grain crop - these flowers originally grew as weeds in wheat and barley fields.
compareHints: Among its knapweed relatives in New England, perennial cornflower stands out with its bright blue-purple color and usually entire leaves. Spotted knapweed has pink-purple flowers and deeply lobed leaves, while black knapweed has purple flowers but much more divided foliage. The single large flower head per stem also distinguishes it from most other knapweeds.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's knapweeds, spotted knapweed is distinguished by those characteristic dark spots or stripes on its flower bracts, while black knapweed has completely dark bracts and cornflower has much larger, showier blue flowers.
Unlike its knapweed cousins that have pink, purple, or yellow flowers, cornflower is the only member of this genus with true electric-blue blooms.

Among its knapweed relatives, brown knapweed stands out with its consistently star-shaped flowers, while black knapweed looks more brush-like and spotted knapweed has more deeply divided leaves with distinctive black-spotted bracts.
Black knapweed is distinguished from spotted knapweed by its solid-colored leaves (spotted knapweed has deeply lobed, almost ferny leaves) and its darker, more fringed flower bracts.
Among New England's knapweeds, Tyrol knapweed is distinguished by its very short-fringed, dark-edged bracts around the flower base.
Giant knapweed stands out dramatically from other New England knapweeds by its massive size and bright yellow color - most other knapweeds have purple, blue, or pink flowers that are much smaller.
